title: Two sentences
hook: I testify there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is His messenger

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger in white who taught by asking, and a new year's line: bring your questions. Today the pillars begin.

Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah. Wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah. If you've ever stood near a mosque at prayer time, you may have heard those words carried over the rooftops in the call to prayer. In English: I testify that there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is His messenger. Two sentences, said in a breath or two. Muslims place them first among the pillars of their faith: the testimony, the shahadah. And the days ahead stay with these two sentences alone.

Start with the verb both sentences begin with. Not I think, not I feel. I testify. I bear witness. It's a witness's word, for someone who has seen something and will say so in front of others. It turns a belief into a statement made out loud, with your name on it. And in the Qur'an, the first to testify isn't a person at all. Pickthall's translation of surah three: "Allah (Himself) is witness that there is no God save Him. And the angels and the men of learning (too are witness)." So a Muslim saying the shahadah joins a line of witnesses that, in the Qur'an's picture, begins with God. Next, the first sentence, about God: there is no god but Allah. A no, then a yes, and each half gets a day of its own. Then the second sentence, about a person: Muhammad is His messenger. It answers a question the first leaves open: if there is one God, how do people know how to live toward Him? Through the messenger, who brought the message and showed it. Last, where the two sentences live. In the call to prayer, out loud, several times a day. Inside the prayer, said quietly while sitting. Whispered by people at the end of their lives. And said by someone becoming Muslim, a day of its own later this week. Short enough for a child to learn, deep enough for a lifetime of asking what each word means. That's why Muslims can say two sentences hold it all.
screen: `ONE ABOUT GOD, ONE ABOUT A PERSON.`
`IN THE CALL, THE PRAYER, THE LAST BREATH.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, say the shahadah once at half your usual speed, stopping on each word long enough to mean it: I testify, no god, but Allah, Muhammad, His messenger. If you're not, simply hear the words in your mind as the words Muslims say, and notice which one you'd most like to ask about. Either way, let the last word fade, and sit in the quiet after it.
Shahadah. The testimony: two sentences that bear witness to one God and His messenger. Today's word.
Your line: two sentences hold it all. A whole faith, short enough to say in one breath. Next, the first word of it: no.

howItsDone: Muslims hear the shahadah in every call to prayer and recite it while sitting in the ritual prayer; some say it on waking and before sleep, and it is the declaration a person makes on becoming Muslim.
